A [shell]{.alert} is the program that runs your commands - The command line gives you [speed, power, reproducibility, and portability]{.alert} - Every command has the same shape: `command options arguments` - Options start with a dash, and they combine: `ls -lah` - `pwd` says where you are, `ls` shows what is there, `cd` moves you - `~` is home, `.` is here, `..` is one level up - `man`, `tldr`, and `cht.sh` when you get stuck ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -70px;"} [![](figures/bash.png){width="60%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/bash.png"} [![](figures/linux-bash.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/linux-bash.png"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The `man` command issue in WSL :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - On Windows WSL, `man` often does not work out of the box - Minimal Ubuntu images ship without the manual pages to save space - You will see `man: command not found`, or `No manual entry for ls` [Possible solutions:]{.alert} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Installation options: - Install the `man-db` and `manpages` packages: ```bash sudo apt update sudo apt install man-db manpages ``` - Alternative installation command: ```bash sudo apt install man ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Testing the installation: - After installation, test with: ```bash man ls man cp man man ``` ::: :::: ::: # Managing your files 🗂 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Managing your files :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"} :::{.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - Once you can navigate, the next step is [managing files]{.alert} - Downloading, unzipping, copying, moving, renaming, deleting - A GUI handles ten files comfortably. It [scales badly]{.alert} to a thousand - The shell does not ask twice. Expect no ["Do you really want to delete this folder of pictures from your anniversary?"]{.alert} 😅 ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/time.jpg){width="250%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/time.jpg"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Create: `mkdir` and `touch` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `mkdir` creates directories: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} mkdir testing ``` ::: - `-p` creates the parent directories too, builds a [whole tree in one command]{.alert}, and never complains if a directory already exists: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} mkdir -p testing02/subdir ``` ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - `touch` creates empty files: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} touch testing/test1.txt testing/test2.txt ``` ::: - On a file that already exists, `touch` only updates its timestamps. [The contents stay untouched]{.alert} - Check that it worked: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ls testing ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` test1.txt test2.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Remove: `rm` and `rmdir` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Let's delete the objects that we just created - Start with one of the `.txt` files, by using `rm` - We could delete all the files at the same time, but you'll see why I want to keep some ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} rm testing/test1.txt ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - The equivalent command for directories is `rmdir` ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} rmdir testing rm: testing: is a directory ``` ::: - `rmdir` only removes [empty]{.alert} directories - For a directory with files in it, use `rm -r` ([recursive]{.alert}). `-r` and `-R` are the same thing - Adding `-f` ([force]{.alert}) skips the confirmation prompt. Leaving it off is safer, but some shells then ask about every single file ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} rm -rf testing ## Success ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Copy: `cp` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} Syntax: `cp object path/newname` - Leave out `newname` and the copy keeps the original one - If something at the destination already has that name, add `-f` to overwrite it ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ## Create new "copies" sub-directory mkdir ./copies ## Now copy across a file (with a new name) cp ./04-more-command-line.qmd ./copies/abc.txt ## Show that we were successful ls ./copies ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` abc.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} Copying a directory needs `-r`, so that everything inside comes along: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} cp -r ./figures ./copies ls ./copies/figures/ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` automation.gif bash.png bookshelf.gif course-repo.png evil-laugh.gif linux-bash.png nano.png next.jpg pipe.gif time.jpg time2.jpg ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Move (and rename): `mv` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"} - Syntax: `mv object path/newname` - Leave out `newname` and the file keeps the one it has ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ## Move a file to see how it works mv ./test.txt ./copies/ ls ./copies ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` abc.txt figures test.txt ``` ::: ::: - Moving a file within the same directory, but under a new name, is how you [rename]{.alert} it ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ## Rename test.txt to test-b.txt mv ./copies/test.txt ./copies/test-b.txt ls ./copies ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` abc.txt figures test-b.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ## Wildcards :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - [Wildcards](http://tldp.org/LDP/GNU-Linux-Tools-Summary/html/x11655.htm) stand in for other characters. Two of them matter most - `*` matches [any number]{.alert} of characters. Use it to act on a whole class of files at once ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # List all files in the "figures" directory that end with ".png" ls figures/*.png ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` figures/bash.png figures/course-repo.png figures/linux-bash.png figures/nano.png ``` ::: ::: - `?` matches [exactly one]{.alert} character. Use it to tell similar names apart ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # List all files in the "figures" directory that start with "tim" and end with ".jpg" ls figures/tim?.jpg ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` figures/time.jpg ``` ::: ::: You can repeat `?`, and [the number of them changes the result]{.alert} ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # List all files in the "figures" directory that start with "time" and end with ".jpg" ls figures/tim??.jpg ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` figures/time2.jpg ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Find :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - `find` locates files and directories by name, size, type, and more - Syntax: `find path(s) -options expression` - `-iname` matches a name, ignoring capitals: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Must use "." to indicate pwd find ./ ../lecture-03/ -iname "*.qmd" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./04-more-command-line.qmd ../lecture-03/03-command-line.qmd ``` ::: ::: - `-size` filters by size, with `k`, `M`, or `G` for kilo, mega, and gigabytes: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Find files larger than 500 KB find . -size +500k | sort # Sort the output ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./04-more-command-line.html ./copies/figures/automation.gif ./copies/figures/bookshelf.gif ./copies/figures/course-repo.png ./copies/figures/evil-laugh.gif ./copies/figures/pipe.gif ./figures/automation.gif ./figures/bookshelf.gif ./figures/course-repo.png ./figures/evil-laugh.gif ./figures/pipe.gif ``` ::: ::: - `-type` filters by kind: `d` for directories, `f` for files: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Find all directories in the parent directory find ./ -type d | sort # Sort the output ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./ ./_extensions ./_extensions/danilofreire ./_extensions/danilofreire/clean ./_extensions/multimodal ./copies ./copies/figures ./figures ./meals ./testing ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Find :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - Combine conditions with `-and`, `-or`, and `-not` (or `!`) - Two conditions side by side already mean `-and` ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Find all .txt files that are larger than 1KB find . -name "*.txt" -size +1k ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./sonnets.txt ./copies/abc.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Find all .txt files OR .qmd files find . -name "*.txt" -or -name "*.qmd" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./sonnets.txt ./testing/test1.txt ./testing/test2.txt ./04-more-command-line.qmd ./copies/abc.txt ./survive.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Find files that are NOT .csv or .gif files find ./figures -not -name "*.csv" -and -not -name "*.gif" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./figures ./figures/time.jpg ./figures/bash.png ./figures/time2.jpg ./figures/linux-bash.png ./figures/next.jpg ./figures/course-repo.png ./figures/nano.png ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Find :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - `-maxdepth n` and `-mindepth n` control how deep the search goes ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Search only in current directory, not subdirectories find . -maxdepth 1 -name "*.txt" # Skip current directory, search only in subdirectories find . -mindepth 2 -name "*.txt" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./sonnets.txt ./survive.txt ./testing/test1.txt ./testing/test2.txt ./copies/abc.txt ``` ::: ::: - `-exec` runs a command on every result. `{}` stands for the filename, and the line must end with `\;` ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Print the size and name of each .txt file find . -name "*.txt" -exec ls -lh {} \; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` -rw-r--r--@ 1 dafreir staff 117K May 8 06:00 ./sonnets.txt -rw-r--r--@ 1 dafreir staff 0B May 8 06:00 ./testing/test1.txt -rw-r--r--@ 1 dafreir staff 0B May 8 06:00 ./testing/test2.txt -rw-r--r--@ 1 dafreir staff 28K Sep 6 19:46 ./copies/abc.txt -rw-r--r--@ 1 dafreir staff 97B May 8 06:00 ./survive.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Count lines in each .csv file find . -name "*.csv" -exec wc -l {} \; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 8 ./meals/mealplan.csv 2 ./meals/tuesday.csv 2 ./meals/monday.csv 2 ./meals/thursday.csv 2 ./meals/wednesday.csv 2 ./meals/saturday.csv 2 ./meals/sunday.csv 2 ./meals/friday.csv ``` ::: ::: ::: # File management exercise 📂 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## File management exercise {#sec-exercise-01} ### I will show you some time-saving tips after the exercise :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Imagine that you are a data analyst working in a new project. The project should have the following structure: ```{.default} project/ │ ├── scripts/ │ ├── preprocessing.py │ ├── analysis.py │ └── visualization.py │ ├── data/ │ ├── raw_data.csv │ └── processed_data.csv │ └── docs/ ├── readme.txt └── notes.txt ``` ::: :::{.column width="50%"} Your tasks: 1. Create the folders and files shown 2. Rename `raw_data.csv` to `input_data.csv` 3. Copy the Python files into a new `project/backup` folder 4. Delete `docs/notes.txt` 5. List the folders in `project`, long format and human-readable sizes 6. Delete everything [[Answer: Appendix 01]{.button}](#sec-appendix-01) ::: ::: ::: ## How to use `{}` to create multiple files or directories :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `{}` expands into several names at once, so one command does the work of many - `touch file{1..3}.txt` creates `file1.txt`, `file2.txt`, `file3.txt` - `mkdir dir{a,b,c}` creates `dira`, `dirb`, `dirc` - It works with any command: `cp`, `mv`, `rm` ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - For example: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} mkdir -p project/{scripts,data,docs} touch project/scripts/{preprocessing,analysis,visualization}.py touch project/data/data{1..5}.csv touch project/docs/{readme.txt,notes.txt} ls project/data ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` data1.csv data2.csv data3.csv data4.csv data5.csv ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ls project/scripts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` analysis.py preprocessing.py visualization.py ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ls project/docs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` notes.txt readme.txt ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Other tips: `&&`, `||` and `tree` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `&&` runs the next command only if the first one [succeeded]{.alert} - `mkdir my-dir && ls my-dir` - `||` runs it only if the first one [failed]{.alert} - `mkdir my-dir || echo "Directory already exists"` - Chain them to handle both cases in one line ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - `tree` draws the structure of a directory - Install it with `brew install tree` on macOS, or `sudo apt-get install tree` on Linux and WSL - [More information here](https://github.com/Old-Man-Programmer/tree) ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} mkdir -p book/{code,data,text}/chapter-{1..3} && \ tree book ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` book ├── code │   ├── chapter-1 │   ├── chapter-2 │   └── chapter-3 ├── data │   ├── chapter-1 │   ├── chapter-2 │   └── chapter-3 └── text ├── chapter-1 ├── chapter-2 └── chapter-3 13 directories, 0 files ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: ::: # Working with text files 📄 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Working with text files :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Data scientists spend [a lot of time with text]{.alert}: scripts, Markdown, CSVs, logs - Python and R are excellent for analysing text, and you will use them later - The shell is excellent at a different job: looking at text, and quickly - It is also already installed, on every machine you will ever log into - The next few slides only scratch the surface ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -30px; margin-left: 50px;"} [![](figures/bookshelf.gif){width="150%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/bookshelf.gif"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Counting text: `wc` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"} - `wc` counts lines, words, and characters, in that order - Let's try it on a file holding all of Shakespeare's sonnets. [Source](http://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1041/pg1041.txt) ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ## Download the file. -o is to specify the output filename # curl -o sonnets.txt https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danilofreire/datasci350/main/lectures/lecture-04/sonnets.txt wc sonnets.txt ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3029 20701 119751 sonnets.txt ``` ::: ::: The character count looks high because `wc` also counts the invisible newline `\n` at the end of every line ::: :::{.callout-note} Download the `sonnets.txt` file at . Click on "Download raw file". Or use `curl` as shown in the code above. [Download curl here](https://curl.se/download.html). ::: ## Read text: `cat` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `cat` ("concatenate") prints the [whole]{.alert} file at once - Fine for short files. Painful for long ones, as you are about to see - `-n` adds line numbers - Shakespeare's sonnets will overflow this slide, which is rather the point 😅 ::: :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} cat -n sonnets.txt ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 ﻿The Project Gutenberg EBook of Shakespeare's Sonnets, by William Shakespeare 2 3 This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere at no cost and with 4 almost no restrictions whatsoever. font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `grep` can search many files at once - This is how you find which file defines a function you are looking for ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} ## To visualise the tree structure tree meals ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` meals ├── friday.csv ├── mealplan.csv ├── monday.csv ├── saturday.csv ├── sunday.csv ├── thursday.csv ├── tuesday.csv └── wednesday.csv 1 directory, 8 files ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - `-r` (recursive) searches a directory and everything under it. Here, every line mentioning "pasta": ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} grep -r "pasta" ./meals/ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./meals/mealplan.csv:monday,muesli,sandwich,pasta ./meals/monday.csv:monday,muesli,sandwich,pasta ``` ::: ::: - `-l` lists only the file names, not the matching lines: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} grep -rl "pasta" ./meals/ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ./meals/mealplan.csv ./meals/monday.csv ``` ::: ::: - `man grep` lists many more. `-i` ignores capitals, which is usually what you want ::: ::: ::: ## Try it yourself! {#sec-exercise-02} :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - Now it's your turn to practice with text files! - Download the text file with Shakespeare's Sonnets from [our repository](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-04/sonnets.txt) or use `curl` as shown before - Go to the terminal and navigate to the directory where you saved the file - Then try to do the following: - Find all lines in sonnets.txt that contain the word "time" - View the last 20 lines in sonnets.txt - Count the number of lines and words in sonnets.txt - [Tricky question:]{.alert} Find all lines in sonnets.txt that [start]{.alert} with "and" - [Super tricky question:]{.alert} Find all lines in sonnets.txt that start with "and" _and_ "And" [[Appendix 02]{.button}](#sec-appendix-02) ::: ## Manipulate text: `sed` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `sed` is a [stream editor]{.alert}. It transforms text as it flows past, from a file or from a pipe - `s/old/new/g` substitutes. `s` is substitute, `g` means every match on the line - On its own it prints the result and leaves the file alone: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} sed 's/Project Gutenberg/Project Googleberg/g' sonnets.txt | head -n 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ﻿The Project Googleberg EBook of Shakespeare's Sonnets, by William Shakespeare This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere at no cost and with almost no restrictions whatsoever. It can delete, insert, and rearrange lines - `d` deletes every line that matches: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} sed '/Project Gutenberg/d' sonnets.txt ``` ::: - To read more about `sed`, check out the [GNU documentation](https://www.gnu.org/software/sed/manual/sed.html) ::: ::: ::: ## Do you want to know more about `sed`? ### Make sure to master regular expressions! :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} **Good starting points are:** - [This chapter](https://effective-shell.com/part-3-manipulating-text/regex-essentials/) discussing regex in the context of the shell - [Regular Expression in Python](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/regex.html) - [This base R regex intro](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/regex.html) - [This vignette from the stringr package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/stringr/vignettes/regular-expressions.html) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} [![](figures/evil-laugh.gif){width="150%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/evil-laugh.gif"} ::: ::: ::: ## Nano: a CLI-based text editor ### For when you need to make quick edits :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `nano` is a simple text editor that runs inside the terminal - Useful for a quick edit when opening VS Code would be overkill, and essential on a remote server - Open a file with `nano filename` - Arrow keys to move, `Ctrl + O` to save, `Ctrl + X` to exit - macOS needs `brew install nano`. WSL usually has it, or `sudo apt install nano` - More in the [GNU documentation](https://www.nano-editor.org/dist/v2.9/nano.html) ::: :::{.column width="50%"} [![Click on the image to enlarge it](figures/nano.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/nano.png"} ::: ::: ::: # Redirects, pipes, and loops 🔁 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Redirects, pipes, and loops :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Small tools become powerful when you connect them - A [pipe]{.alert} feeds one command's output into the next, like `%>%` in R - A [redirect]{.alert} sends output into a file instead of onto the screen - A [loop]{.alert} repeats a command over a list - This is the Unix philosophy in practice: one thing done well, many times over ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} [![](figures/pipe.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pipe.gif"} ::: ::: ::: ## Redirect: `>` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - `>` sends output to a file instead of the screen - `echo` just prints a message, so it makes an easy example: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} echo "At first, I was afraid, I was petrified" ``` ::: To save it instead, redirect it into a filename of your choice: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} echo "At first, I was afraid, I was petrified" > survive.txt find survive.txt ## Show that it now exists ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` survive.txt ``` ::: ::: - `>>` [appends]{.alert} to a file. `>` [overwrites]{.alert} whatever was there - Mixing the two up is a common way to lose work ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} echo "'Kept thinking I could never live without you by my side" >> survive.txt cat survive.txt ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` At first, I was afraid, I was petrified 'Kept thinking I could never live without you by my side ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Pipes: `|` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - `|` takes the output of the command on its left and feeds it to the one on its right - Chain simple operations and you get a complex one, with no script and no temporary files - An example using commands you already know: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Read the sonnets.txt file, find all lines that contain the word "time", and count the number of lines and words cat sonnets.txt | grep "time" | wc -lw ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 57 469 ``` ::: ::: - Each stage does one job, and the data flows left to right ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # Another example: find all lines in sonnets.txt that contain the word "love" and print the first 5 lines cat sonnets.txt | grep "love" | head -n 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Of his self-love to stop posterity? Calls back the lovely April of her prime; Unthrifty loveliness, why dost thou spend The lovely gaze where every eye doth dwell, No love toward others in that bosom sits ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Iteration with *for* loops :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} - A `for` loop repeats an operation over a list - It works much like a `for` loop in Python or R - The `$` marks a variable, so `$i` is the current item - Basic syntax: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} for i in LIST do OPERATION $i ## the $ sign indicates a variable in bash done ``` ::: - `;` ends a statement, so the whole loop fits on one line: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} for i in LIST; do OPERATION $i; done ``` ::: Semicolons are not limited to loops.
